dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?

Hi, yes, good afternoon. My name is Carmen Herrera. Um, so I'm calling because my neighbor, the one next door, he's putting up a fence. They had the guys out yesterday, in all that mud, after the rain, and the snow before that, you know, that whole mess from the weekend. And I thought, well, I've been wanting one too.
Okay. Good to meet you, Carmen. Which address are we talking about?

392 Bacheller Street. Fifth Ward. And honestly my sister-in-law had a fence once, a wooden one, and it fell over in a wind, so I don't want wood. Anyway. I want the black aluminum, the kind that looks like iron but isn't. Five feet tall.
Black aluminum, five feet. Got it. And is this for the front yard, the back, or around the whole property?

Oh, um, mostly the back and down along the side. Not the front. Well, maybe a little of the front, I haven't decided. My friend Dolores, she gave me a list of questions to ask, hold on, I have it here somewhere. It's in my purse. Okay, no, wait, it's on the fridge. I'm in the car.
That's fine, take your time. We can go through it as you think of things.

Okay. So the main one, I think, is do I even need a permit? Because my neighbor, I don't know if he got one. And is there a height where it stops needing one? Like if it's under four feet or something? I heard that somewhere.

In general, a fence does need a permit here, and height is one of the things that matters. Since yours would be five feet, I'd plan on applying. I can't tell you a cutoff off the top of my head, but at five feet you'd want to go through the process either way.
So even if it was shorter I might still need one? I thought it was either or.
It can depend on the height and where on the lot it goes, so the front section matters too. That's why I asked. Front yards are usually treated differently from the back.
Oh. Okay. So I should decide about the front part first. That makes sense, kind of. I'm sorry, I'm still a little mixed up, but okay.
No problem. When you apply, you'll show where the fence goes on a sketch of your property, and the materials and height. Do you have a survey or a plot plan?
A survey? We got something from the bank when we bought the house, years ago, with the lines on it. Is that it? Or is a survey a different thing?
That could be it if it shows the property lines and the house. Bring it in or send a photo and we can see if it's usable.
Okay, good. And how long does it take? To get approved? Dolores said it took her cousin like two months but that was in Providence.

I don't want to give you a number I can't stand behind. For a simple residential fence it's usually not long, but it depends on how busy we are and whether your application is complete. A complete one moves faster. If you stop by or call back once you have the sketch, someone can give you a better idea.
So not months necessarily. Okay. And I shouldn't order the fence until I hear back, right?
Right, I'd wait for the approval before ordering or having anyone start digging.
Okay. Let me just look at the list, I think there was one more. Oh, whether the neighbor needs to sign something? Or is that only if the fence is on the line?

Good question. If it's on or near the line, where it sits matters, and that's something the inspector can talk you through when you bring the sketch. Should I take your number in case someone from the office wants to follow up?
Yes, it's 401-555-0185. That's my cell, so if it cuts out just call back.
Got it, 401-555-0185. I'll note that you're at 392 Bacheller about a black aluminum fence, five feet, back and side, front undecided.
Yes, that's it exactly. Thank you, Anita. I think I understand. Mostly. Thank you.
You're welcome, Carmen. Have a good afternoon.
